title: Given an array of `n` integers in the range `1` to `n` where some numbers appear once and some appear exactly twice, return all the numbers that appear twice, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (the output list excluded).
shortTitle: Find all Duplicate Numbers (Every Value Appearing Twice in 1..n)
keyPoints: Place each value v at index v-1 using Cyclic Sort with a duplicate-safe guard to avoid infinite swaps.
After placement, every slot where value != index+1 holds a duplicate value (the stranded value).
Collect the stranded values (not the indices) to get all duplicates.
The dual: scanning for index+1 gives the missing numbers, scanning for the stored value gives the duplicates.
The negative-marking alternative flips the sign at index abs(v)-1 and reports v when the sign is already negative.
Both approaches are O(n) time and O(1) extra space (excluding the output).

s1_definition.oneliner: Place v at index v-1; every stranded value where value != index+1 is a duplicate.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Problem** – n integers in range 1..n; some appear once, some twice. Return all that appear twice in O(n) time and O(1) space.
- **Cyclic Sort** – place each value v at index v-1 with a value-comparison guard to prevent infinite swaps.
- **Stranded values** – after placement, any slot where value != index+1 holds a duplicate that was pushed out of its home.
- **Dual property** – on the same sorted array, scanning for index+1 gives missing numbers; scanning for stored value gives duplicates.
- **Alternative** – negative marking flips the sign at index abs(v)-1; a second flip reports the duplicate.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India expects one receipt per numbered slot 1 to n, but some receipts were printed twice. A clerk files each receipt in its matching slot. Whatever receipt is stranded in a wrong slot at the end is a receipt that got printed an extra time.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding all numbers that appear twice in an array over the range 1 to n is the mirror image of finding all missing numbers, and I solve both with the same Cyclic Sort placement loop. I place each value at the index equal to the value minus one, using the value-comparison swap guard so duplicates do not trap the loop. After that single pass, every slot that does not hold its proper index-plus-one is stranded because a duplicate crowded it out, and the value sitting in that stranded slot is a duplicate.

The elegant part is the dual nature: on the identical array after placement, one scan for index-plus-one yields the missing numbers while another scan for the stored value yields the duplicates. That is why I prefer Cyclic Sort over the negative-marking trick, which can only answer one of the two questions per pass.

The negative-marking approach is a valid alternative: for each value, negate the element at the corresponding index, and if it is already negative, the value is a duplicate. Both approaches are O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

In my project at the National Bank of India, this audited receipt print runs. The printer occasionally emitted a numbered receipt twice, and finance needed the full list of double-printed receipt numbers to void them before the settlement window closed.

Remember one sentence: after Cyclic Sort placement, every slot where value does not equal index+1 holds a duplicate value, and scanning for stored values gives all duplicates in O(n) time.
